function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script).  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that you’ll need to add to the repository.

> **NOTE** – The helper functions in the “Tools” section are meant for *Python* projects.  
> Since this repository is a Node.js app, I’ll hand‑craft the Dockerfile and the GitHub Actions workflow instead of calling those functions.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image as the base
FROM node:18-slim

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first (for caching)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-slim` is a small, production‑ready image.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from the lockfile.  
> * The app listens on port **3000** (the default for many Node.js starter projects).

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-deployment.yaml` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry/tag
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 2 replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the app on port 80 inside the cluster (forwarded to container port 3000).  
> * Uses a `ClusterIP` service – change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout source
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          echo ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin
          docker push ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Tag latest
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        run: |
          docker tag ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
          docker push ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Key points**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Installs Node.js 18, runs tests, builds a Docker image, and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry.  
> * Tags the image as `latest` only when the commit lands on `main`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new **Dockerfile** in the repo root.  
* A **k8s-deployment.yaml** file.  
* A **.github/workflows/ci.yml** file.  
* The GitHub Actions tab should show a successful run for the latest commit on `main`.

That’s it! 🎉 If you run into any issues (e.g., Docker Hub credentials, missing tests), let me know and I can help troubleshoot.
